home.flowTitle: The 6 things I'll do for you
home.flowIntro: A clear process, transparent service, a two-way choice. Every step is explained — we only move on once you're satisfied.

flowSteps.d: It starts with getting to know each other. I'll briefly introduce my professional background and answer the family-protection or retirement questions on your mind. Only with mutual understanding can real trust — and a long-term relationship — begin.

Every family's finances are different, so protection can't be one-size-fits-all. I'll help you complete a detailed family finance questionnaire: income and expenses, savings and investments, loans and debts, existing cover, family goals and a comfortable budget range.

Owning many policies doesn't mean owning the right ones. I'll lay out your cover types, sums assured, terms and total premiums in charts, review the gaps, and — together with your life stage and values — identify the cover you genuinely need.

You won't get a pile of product documents and jargon, but 2–3 tailored options for your family, explained in plain language with diagrams. In person or by video, I encourage questions — we only continue once you're satisfied.

Once you decide, I'll walk you through the application step by step: filling and submitting documents, health declarations, and reading the contract terms and exclusions. If there's loading or an exclusion, I'll help with communication and appeals — declare cleanly, claim with peace of mind.

Signing isn't the end of the service — it's the start of a long-term one. I review your policies each year to keep pace with life changes, help update beneficiaries, address and payment methods, and stay with you through key moments: a new baby, schooling, buying a home, preparing for retirement. If a claim arises, I'll help coordinate it as fast as I can.

about.title: Yuan Yuan
about.subtitle: Yuan Yuan SG · Make protection clear, arrange the future steadily
about.quickBody:
I'm Yuan Yuan, an AIA Wealth Manager in Singapore, with a Master's from NTU and a past career in product design at Great Eastern and Grab.

Having worked hands-on on insurance apps, online claims and customer experience, I care about one thing more than most advisers: whether clients truly understand the cover they've bought.

Today I focus on helping families in Singapore make sense of medical, critical illness, life, retirement cash flow and legacy planning.
about.intro: I'm Yuan Yuan, an AIA Wealth Manager in Singapore and an MDRT member. I've worked in insurance and finance in Singapore for over 6 years — from helping design an insurer's app and online claims system at the country's largest insurer, to planning insurance and finances for families myself today. I've served families from Singapore, Malaysia, Australia, Turkey and beyond. Their backgrounds differ, but their hope is the same: to put down roots here and live with peace of mind. I believe wealth isn't built overnight, but through the right plan — making protection solid, step by step, and arranging the future steadily.
about.section1Title: From product design to wealth management
about.section1Body:
I didn't start out in this field.

After graduating from Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications in 2013, I came to Singapore for a Master's in Digital Media Technology at NTU. For nearly a decade after, I worked as a product designer —

At DeNA, a leading Japanese mobile game company, I ran planning and operations for a Marvel game, coordinating across Tokyo, Singapore, Hanoi and North America. At Great Eastern, Singapore's largest insurer, I led a six-person UX team in redesigning the official app and online claims system for 2.5 million policyholders. Later I joined the Southeast Asian super-app Grab, leading design for the GrabFood merchant platform and GrabExpress.

Through all of it, I kept one habit: no matter how busy, I always made time to document and reflect. It's what let me see my own path clearly at every turning point.
about.section2Body:
If you've seen my résumé, this might surprise you: why would someone with nearly a decade in product design — at DeNA, Great Eastern, Grab — turn to insurance?

It starts with a prejudice.

Before entering this field, I knew nothing about insurance and was, frankly, biased against it — I thought of it as a favour, a tangle of fine print. Then, during my years at Great Eastern, I designed the company's customer app and online claims system, walked through the entire journey from application to claim, and personally interviewed hundreds of policyholders, agents and claims staff.

I saw the industry as it really is: many people buy insurance yet never understand what they're actually covered for; many practitioners favour marketing over service, acquisition over after-care — once a policy is sold, the client can't find them again. Behind that mess lies countless families' misunderstanding of, and disappointment with, the word "protection."

In 2023, returning from maternity leave at Grab, my department was dissolved. Rather than rush to the next job, I used the pause to seriously consider what I wanted. A seasoned career coach, after getting to know me, suggested something unexpected: become a wealth adviser. She said I was gentle, methodical, numbers-sensitive and logical — exactly the foundation this work needs.

In that moment I felt a strange sense of destiny: wasn't I once exactly the person who was biased against insurance? If even I could be won over by genuinely professional, genuinely client-first service, couldn't I become that kind of adviser too — and change how more people see this industry?

So I chose AIA, and a team whose client-first philosophy matched my own. My approach is simple: review first, then talk solutions, and never pester friends. When I'm not with clients, I spend my time sharing real, useful knowledge on social media, and let the people who need me come to me. Earning clients this way means I have to be genuinely good — that's the only way to be seen and trusted.

And it works — in my first year, on word of mouth and referrals alone, I earned MDRT membership.
about.section3Title: Building a reputation through professionalism and care
about.section3Body:
My approach is simple: move forward in small, solid steps.

I'm not chasing speed. I'm chasing the day when, years from now, a client mentioned in passing can say with conviction: "Oh, Yuan Yuan — she's a trustworthy, dependable adviser who really knows her stuff."
about.mediaBody: I don't like to intrude — but I'm far from passive. When I'm not with clients, I do one thing: take the complex, easily-misunderstood parts of insurance and finance, and explain them in plain language anyone can follow.

cases.title: Real planning, real considerations
cases.intro: The following are anonymised summaries of real client situations. All identifying details have been removed and figures masked; they're shared only to illustrate the planning approach.
cases.msNote: Every plan I make follows the basic financial-planning principles of MoneySense, by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) — protection first, then growth, always within your means.

list.tag: New to the workforce · Is group cover enough?
list.title: New to Singapore with only company group cover — do I really need personal insurance?
list.profile: 28, EP holder, newly joined a tech firm in Singapore, single, parents back home. Annual income around S$90,000, with some savings but an emergency fund that's still thin.
list.existing: Only company group medical and accident cover, which lapses on leaving or changing jobs; no personal policies.
list.worry: Afraid that a serious illness or accident would not only interrupt income, but also take away the group cover along with the job.
list.notAdvice: I didn't start by recommending savings or investment products. At this stage his emergency fund was thin and personal protection was nearly blank, so chasing long-term returns wouldn't pay off.
list.firstAdvice: First, on a budget under 15% of income, build three foundational layers: (1) a personal Integrated Shield Plan — portable and lifelong, unaffected by job changes; (2) personal accident cover; (3) an early critical-illness policy locked in while young and rates are low.
list.whyOrder: Company group cover is "borrowed protection" — almost nothing truly belongs to him. While he's young and healthy and rates are low, covering high-impact risks like medical and critical illness matters more than rushing into investments — and costs less.
list.outcome: On a manageable budget, he now has a first layer of protection that's truly his own, in place even if he changes jobs or leaves the company. Investing can wait until his emergency fund and cash flow are steadier.

list.tag: Newlyweds with a mortgage · Protecting the home
list.title: We bought a home and took on a mortgage — if one of us is hit, can the other hold on?
list.profile: Both in their early 30s, dual income, one PR and one citizen. Just bought a home with a sizeable mortgage; no children yet.
list.existing: Each has hospitalisation and accident cover from before marriage, but no critical illness or life cover.
list.worry: Their biggest fear: "if one of us goes down, can the other carry the mortgage alone, or would we be forced to sell?"
list.notAdvice: I didn't suggest adding large savings or investment plans right away. Their biggest risk wasn't "money not growing fast enough" — it was "family responsibility suddenly falling on one person."
list.firstAdvice: Close two gaps first: (1) a mortgage-reducing term assurance covering the outstanding balance, one each, so that if one passes away or is totally disabled, the payout clears the mortgage directly; (2) critical-illness cover each, so that if one falls ill there's money to replace income and cover recovery. Total premiums kept within 15% of household income.
list.whyOrder: The mortgage is the heaviest fixed responsibility at this stage and must be hedged first. Cover the worst case with relatively low premiums before talking about savings and growth — the order can't be reversed.
list.outcome: Now, whichever partner is affected, the home is safe and the other won't be crushed by the mortgage. With the foundation secured, they began a long-term savings plan with peace of mind.

list.tag: Family with a child · Getting the order right
list.title: Now that we have a baby — insure the child first, or shore up the parents' cover?
list.profile: Parents in their 30s, settled in Singapore, upper-middle household income. Baby just born; relatives are keen to set up insurance and an education fund for the child quickly.
list.existing: Both parents have hospitalisation cover, but critical-illness and life cover are still short relative to family responsibilities; the child has no policy yet.
list.worry: They worry about the child's health and future education fund, while sensing that "the adults are the ones who actually earn" — but unsure how to set priorities.
list.notAdvice: I didn't suggest piling insurance or a large education fund onto the child first. The child's biggest protection is the parents themselves; investing heavily in the child while the adults have gaps puts the cart before the horse.
list.firstAdvice: Three steps in order: (1) first shore up the parents' (especially the main earner's) critical-illness and life cover; (2) then set up basic hospitalisation and accident cover for the child, while early-life underwriting is simple and rates low; (3) finally, once the first two are solid, start a long-term, steady education savings plan for the child.
list.whyOrder: If the family's main earner is hit, it's the child's life and education that suffer most. Fortify the "adults" line of defence first, and the child's protection and education fund will truly have something to rest on. This is the order MoneySense consistently emphasises.
list.outcome: With the parents' gaps closed, they set up hospitalisation, accident and a long-term education plan for the child with confidence — clear on the role and priority of every piece.

list.tag: High-income family · Retirement cash flow & USD savings
list.title: 40, comfortable income — how should I design retirement cash flow and USD savings?
list.profile: Early 40s, senior manager, stable career at peak earning years. Married with children, ageing parents, health and critical-illness cover already fairly complete. Has funds not needed in the short term, wanting both steady growth and preparation for retirement and legacy.
list.existing: Complete medical, critical-illness, accident and some life cover; but no clear long-term cash-flow and wealth-succession arrangement.
list.worry: Two concerns: that income may stop after retirement and lower his living standard; and that idle cash is slowly eroded by inflation — yet he doesn't want too much investment volatility.
list.notAdvice: I didn't suggest putting all the money into high-volatility investments to "chase a high return." His goal is certainty and flexibility, not a gamble.
list.firstAdvice: With protection already complete, design a steady mid-to-long-term savings / participating plan as the core of retirement cash flow: income can be drawn from an agreed term as needed, un-withdrawn amounts keep accumulating, and unused value can pass to family as a death benefit. If there's a need for USD exposure, a USD savings plan can diversify single-currency risk.
list.whyOrder: What he lacks at this stage isn't protection, but a "certain, flexible, inheritable" long-term cash-flow arrangement. Lock in the retirement floor with steady tools first, then consider a smaller portion for flexible growth — "steady" before "offence."
list.outcome: He has a relatively certain, reversible cash flow for retirement: start it early if needed, or let the funds keep growing if not, with unused value left to family. Note: dividends and drawdown figures are non-guaranteed; the insurer's official documents and illustrations prevail.

list.title: Plenty of property, but the stock market is exhausting — how do I get steady passive income?
list.profile: A family in their 40s with 3 investment properties, CPF maxed out, and cash flow coming mainly from rent. Not interested in the stock market and with no energy to watch it, they want a low-maintenance, steady passive income — and more time for the family.
list.existing: Assets heavily concentrated in property and CPF; basic protection is largely complete, but liquid assets and tools that generate steady cash flow are limited.
list.worry: Worried that assets are over-concentrated in property with poor liquidity; yet wary of diving into the stock market, which is draining and stressful and eats into quality of life.
list.notAdvice: I didn't suggest buying more property, nor high-volatility investments that need constant watching. What he lacked wasn't more assets, but "low-maintenance, steady cash flow he can hold in hand."
list.firstAdvice: With protection already complete, allocate part of the liquid funds to a steady participating savings / fund to build a relatively smooth mid-to-long-term cash flow; at the same time, moderately reduce reliance on a single property market so the overall asset mix is more balanced.
list.whyOrder: His core wish is to "give time back to the family." Solving cash flow and over-concentration with low-maintenance tools matters more than adding yet another asset that needs hands-on management.
list.outcome: Without adding management burden, he gained a relatively steady source of cash flow, and his assets are no longer over-bet on a single market. Note: dividends are non-guaranteed, depending on the insurer's actual performance; the official policy document prevails.

consult.faqIntro: Grouped by topic — start with what matters most to you. For some questions I've also made detailed write-ups or videos on Xiaohongshu and WeChat Channels.

items.q: What does the first consultation cover? Do I need to prepare documents?
items.a: We'll start from the questions you care about most and get to know each other. You don't need to prepare complex documents in advance — just bring any existing policies and I'll help you make sense of them.

Six steps in full: build trust → gather information → needs analysis → design the plan → help you apply → lifelong service. I've made a visual guide breaking down each step, available on my Xiaohongshu profile.

items.q: What if I'm not happy with the plan?
items.a: If you're not happy, we keep refining until you genuinely agree. We only move to the next step once you're satisfied — it's a two-way choice.

items.q: Given Singapore's risks, is my cover enough?
items.a: I've recorded a video on the common protection gaps for families in Singapore, explained with local medical and accident scenarios — available on WeChat Channels.

items.q: How should critical illness and medical insurance work together?
items.a: I've put together a visual guide with a real budget example showing how critical illness and medical complement each other, so you avoid overlapping cover and wasted money.

items.q: What should I watch out for in health declarations?
items.a: Incorrect declarations can affect future claims. I'll use my experience to help you get the key wording right — truthful and to your benefit. Declare cleanly, claim with peace of mind.

items.q: I want to start planning for retirement — where do I begin?
items.a: I have a video specifically on designing retirement cash flow, working backwards from your goal to how much to set aside each month — available on WeChat Channels.

items.q: I hold USD assets — should I worry about estate tax?
items.a: Non-US persons holding US-situated assets may face estate-tax exposure. I've made a write-up on common scenarios and feasible insurance structures; specifics still defer to professional tax and legal advice.

items.q: How is insurance used for wealth succession?
items.a: Insurance can designate beneficiaries and bypass parts of the process, making it a common long-term succession tool. The structure should be designed around your family; matters involving wills and trusts will be advised on by the relevant licensed or professional institutions.

items.q: Just got my EP — what cover should I set up first?
items.a: I've put together a visual guide to protection priorities for a new resident's first year, from medical and accident to income replacement, explained stage by stage.

items.q: Is it worth opening an SRS retirement account?
items.a: I've recorded a video on the tax advantages of SRS and who it suits, and noted the change to the statutory withdrawal age from July 2026.

items.q: Will CRS / tax reporting affect me?
items.a: EP holders have corresponding reporting obligations. I'll flag the points to note; for specific tax advice I'll also point you to a qualified tax professional.
